title: Pictures and Text Working Together
keyIdea: In a book, the words and the pictures work together. Sometimes the picture shows what the words say. Often it adds more: what a character looks like, the weather, the place, or how a moment feels. Some books tell a second story only in the pictures, so you need to read both. In fact books, a label names a part of a picture or diagram, and a caption is a sentence that tells you what the picture shows.

kid: Read the words. Then look at the picture. The words say, "Max the dog wants to play." The picture shows rain. The words never said rain! The picture must still match the words: a hot sun, not a moon.
Pictures can change how a page feels. "Mia walked into the woods." A dark, stormy picture feels scary. A sunny one feels happy. The words stay the same.
In some books, the pictures tell a secret. The words only talk about Hen. The pictures show a fox following her!
Fact books have labels and captions. A label names a part, like wing. A caption says what the picture shows.
adult: This is reading comprehension through the picture-text relationship. US Common Core RL.1.7 asks children to use illustrations and details to describe characters, setting or events, RI.1.6 to tell information from pictures apart from information in the words, and RL.3.7 to explain how illustrations create mood or emphasise a character or setting. RI.2.7 adds how images such as diagrams clarify a text. England's Key Stage 1 reading asks children to discuss what they read and check it makes sense, which includes the pictures.

Researchers on picturebooks describe three main relationships. The picture can match the words, extend them by adding detail the words leave out, or even counterpoint them by telling something different. Pat Hutchins' Rosie's Walk is a classic case: the words follow Rosie the hen round the farmyard and never mention the fox, which appears only in the illustrations.

Common mistakes: reading only the words and skipping the pictures, treating pictures as decoration, assuming the picture just repeats the words, and mixing up labels (a single word naming a part) with captions (a sentence about the whole picture). A common adult slip is covering the pictures to make a child 'really read'; for comprehension, ask "What does the picture tell us that the words do not?"

In the lab your child sorts facts by whether they came from the words, the picture or both, illustrates three sentences by choosing matching pictures, changes sky, weather and a face to make the same sentence feel scary and then happy, finds the fox the words never mention on three pages, and labels a bee before choosing its caption.

familyTip: At story time, pause on a page and ask, "What can you see in the picture that the words did not tell us?" Try Rosie's Walk by Pat Hutchins together and let your child tell you the fox's side of the story.

visual.caption: Label or caption? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: A bee drinks nectar from a flower.
A frog can jump far on its long back legs.
The castle was built about 900 years ago.
Penguins huddle together to keep warm.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: words or picture, be the illustrator, set the mood of a page, find what the words leave out, label a bee and pick its caption.

practice.prompt: The words say "Ben went to the park." The picture shows Ben in a red coat, kicking leaves. What do you learn only from the picture?
practice.hint: Which fact is not in the words at all?
practice.explain: The words tell you where Ben went. The red coat and the leaves come only from the picture.

practice.prompt: A picture has {n} ducks. The words say "Some ducks swam." How many ducks does the picture tell you about?
practice.hint: The words say "some". Count the ducks in the picture.
practice.explain: The words do not give a number, but the picture shows {n} ducks. The picture adds that detail.

practice.prompt: The words say "It was a cold, snowy night." Which picture matches?
practice.hint: Find the words cold, snowy and night in the picture.
practice.explain: Snow and a moon match "cold, snowy night". The beach and the hot garden do not.

practice.prompt: A bee diagram has {k} labels. Each label names one part. How many parts are named?
practice.explain: {k} labels name {k} parts. A label is a word that names a part of the picture.

pool.prompt: Can a picture tell you something the words do not?
choices: No, it only copies the words
pool.hint: Think of the rain in Max's picture.
pool.explain: Pictures often add details the words leave out, like the weather or what someone looks like.

pool.prompt: Same words: "Sam opened the gate." One picture is dark with shadows. One is bright and sunny. Which feels scary?
pool.hint: How do dark and shadows make you feel?
pool.explain: The words are the same, but the dark picture with shadows sets a scary mood.

choices: A sentence that tells what a picture shows
pool.hint: It sits under a photo in a fact book.
pool.explain: A caption is a sentence about the picture. A label is one word naming a part, and the book's name is its title.

pool.prompt: In Rosie's Walk, the words never say "fox". How do we know a fox is there?
pool.hint: Look where the words do not.
pool.explain: The fox is only in the pictures. That is why you need to read the pictures too.

pool.prompt: A page in a fact book has {p} photos. Each photo has one caption under it. How many captions are on the page?
pool.hint: One caption goes with each photo.
pool.explain: {p} photos, one caption each, makes {p} captions. Each caption tells what its photo shows.

pool.prompt: The words say "Lola was happy." Which picture matches?
pool.hint: What does a happy face look like?
pool.explain: A smile matches happy. A picture that does not match the words would confuse the reader.

pool.prompt: A diagram of a plant has {a} labels on the flower and {b} on the roots. How many labels in all?
pool.hint: Add the labels on both parts.
pool.explain: {a} and {b} make {=a+b} labels. Each one names a part of the plant.

pool.prompt: Why should you look at the pictures as well as read the words?
choices: They can add to the story
They always say the same as the words
pool.hint: Think of the fox following Hen.
pool.explain: Pictures can add detail, set the mood or tell a second story, so reading both gives you the whole story.
